paragraphs: A Tyrrhenian trader is in with wine and Campanian ware, and he is giving away a tale before he has sold a single jar: the Romans have fought the greatest battle anyone can remember, at a place called Sentinum, in the hills on the far side of Italy.
Samnites and Gauls stood together against two consular armies, forty thousand men on a side, he says, and holds up his hands for the size of it.

For the price of a cup he gives you the whole of it. The Senones, the same Gauls who burned Rome in our great-grandfathers' time, came down with their chariots and broke the Roman left. The consul Decius, seeing his line go, spoke the old vow that gives a man's own life to the gods below together with the enemy's host, and rode into the Gauls to die.

The other consul, Fabius, held, turned the Samnites and stormed their camp; their general Gellius Egnatius fell at its gate. The trader swears to twenty-five thousand of the enemy dead. The old men on the quay say only this: the Gauls have been beaten in the open field, and every Gaul from the Rhodanos to the Alps will hear of it before the grapes are in.

chronicle: A trader up from the Tyrrhenian Sea brought word of Rome's victory over the Samnites and the Gauls at Sentinum.

paragraphs: You leave him to his audience. By evening every wine-shop on the Lakydon has the Romans winning the battle twice over.
